input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane while vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. In this study, two membranes, one polymer and one zeolite, were compared on a single duty: a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. Each membrane was tested on the same feed, at the same temperature, with vacuum drawn on the permeate side throughout, ensuring that the comparison is between membranes and not between test conditions. Performance is stated in terms of flux and the separation factor. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 240; over 500 h, however, its flux decreased by 14%. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 0.9 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 420; over 500 h its flux was unchanged within measurement error. In other words, the polymer passes more water through each unit of area and separates the mixture less sharply, and the flux it starts with is not held. The zeolite passes less, separates more sharply, and holds its flux across the run. For a duty that values throughput, the polymer's higher flux is paid for with the weaker separation and the decline; for a duty that values the separation, the zeolite's lower flux is the price of the sharper, stable performance. It is notable that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and a comparison that reports only the first two ranks the polymer first and says nothing about the third. The tested scope is admittedly narrow: one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h, so the ranking is established at that composition and inside 500 h, and at no other composition or longer duration.
